title: Arrival surge spectrogram scratch
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory notebook-style notes for using time-frequency (spectrogram) views of request arrivals to understand recurring micro-burst structure and its correlation with p95/p99 latency spikes. Goal is to find signatures we can detect cheaply in proxy telemetry and use to trigger short-term routing/scale actions.

Setup (env):
- cluster: dev-fleet-3 (4xA100, vgpus disabled, local KV cache enabled)
- model: opt-6.7b-quant (running as opt-6.7b-q8_0)
- bench tool: /bench/ingress-sim v0.9 (custom arrival generator)
- telemetry: Prometheus scrape + short window traces to jaeger, and payload-level timestamping (ingress_ts, enqueue_ts, start_infer_ts, finish_ts)

Commands used (examples):
- run spectrogram capture: ./ingress-sim --pattern clustered --mean-qps 120 --burst-mean 800 --burst-std 200 --burst-duration 200ms --duration 30m --emit-ts csv > arrivals-120-clustered.csv
- convert to spectrogram: python viz/spectrogram_from_timestamps.py arrivals-120-clustered.csv --window 2s --overlap 90 --fft-bin-ms 50 --out arrivals-120-clust-spec.png

Key parameters tried:
- mean QPS: 40, 120, 350
- arrival models: poisson, cluster (Weibull inter-arrival), periodic-sawtooth, zipfian spikes
- window lengths: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 5s
- freq resolution: 20-200ms per bin

Observations (raw):
- Clustered arrivals (burst mean 800 req/min, 200ms burst duration) produce strong high-frequency bands in the spectrogram around 100-300ms periodicity (visible as horizontal bands). These align with p95 spikes in the latency trace.
- Poisson arrivals appear as a more broadband, lower-magnitude spectrogram — no persistent narrowband features. Latency tail still exists but is less synchronized across slots.
- Sawtooth/ramp patterns create low-frequency energy (1-10s) and correlate with gradual SLO drift (p50->p95 widening) rather than sharp p99 spikes.
- When KV cache priming is happening (first 60s after cold start), spectrogram shows mixed high-frequency transients that decay as cache warms.

Representative numbers (from run arrivals-120-clustered):
- baseline mean latency: 42ms
- within bursts p95: 210ms, p99: 520ms
- outside bursts p95: 48ms, p99: 90ms
- observed burst duty cycle: ~7-12% over 30m run

Small CSV snippet (timestamps are ms since epoch, simplified):
ts,delta_from_prev,queue_ms,start_infer_ms,finish_ms
1709801230012,120,2,12,54
1709801230132,5,0,10,46
1709801230137,3,1,11,50
1709801230140,200,3,14,58
...

Interpretation / hypotheses:
- Narrowband high-frequency energy (~100-300ms) likely indicates bursty client-side retries or multiplexed workers releasing batched requests synchronously. When many warm requests hit concurrently they amplify queueing and cause transient p99 tails.
- Poisson-like noise still causes tail latency due to resource saturation but less synchronized contention — easier to smooth with batching and small autoscale windows.
- Spectrograms can be computed from ingress timestamps cheaply (sliding-window FFT on counts per 50ms bin). We can use energy in the 50-300ms band as a cheap heuristic to declare a "micro-burst" state.

Detection idea (cheap):
- maintain circular buffer of per-50ms request counts (length 128 bins = 6.4s window)
- compute 1-2 tap FFT (or Go DSP library) and monitor magnitude in bins corresponding to 50ms-500ms periodicity
- if magnitude > threshold for 3 consecutive windows, mark micro-burst and trigger: transient route to spare pool, increase short-term concurrency cap, or enable rapid coalescing.

Notes to self (open questions):
- How sensitive is the detection to bin size and window length? Tradeoff: detection latency vs noise.
- What about clients that intentionally multiplex at ~100ms (e.g., browser batching) — false positives? Need client-ID heuristics.
- Does this work across multi-tenant fleets? Need tenant-normalized thresholds.
- CPU overhead for incremental FFT on proxies — prototype in Go is next step (see linked PR).

Artifacts:
- spectrogram images: gdrive:1a2b3c_arrivals-120-clust.png (attached to PR), gdrive:1a2b3d_arrivals-350-zipf.png
- raw CSVs: gdrive-csv:arrivals-120-clustered.csv
- bench script: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks/tree/main/ingress-sim

Next steps / TODO:
- implement incremental FFT detector in proxy (Go) and run A/B on canary cluster for 24h (low-risk traffic)
- tune thresholds per-tenant using historical traces (sample from last 30 days)
- add fallback logic to prefer routing to spare pool only if concurrent CPU utilization < 65%
- write short draft for product team: "Detecting micro-bursts via ingress spectrograms" (one-pager)

End of scratch notes.

Questions for Mira/Ethan at sync:
- Mira: can we get 48h of per-50ms ingress counts for the east-prod fleet?
- Ethan: any objections to adding a small FFT lib to proxy binary vs separate sidecar?

(keeping this intentionally terse — will expand into a full experiment runbook if detector looks promising)
